34  Markov Chains, Continuous Generators, and the CME

(Markov thread) The exponential action now carries additional meaning: its entries are transition probabilities and its column sums preserve total mass. Truncation is therefore not an arbitrary projection, because leaked mass becomes an observable error certificate.

Markov chains model random systems where transitions depend only on the current state. Discrete-time systems evolve via column-stochastic matrices \(\bx^{(k+1)}=\bP\bx^{(k)}\). Continuous-time Markov jump processes evolve via infinitesimal generators \(\dot{\bp}(t)=\bA\bp(t)\), leading to the Chemical Master Equation. Large or infinite state spaces require projection onto finite subgenerators with rigorous 1-norm leakage bounds.

34.1 Discrete-Time Markov Chains

NoteDefinition: Probability Vector

A vector \(\bx\in\fR^n\) is a probability vector if \[ \begin{align} x_i\geq 0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^n x_i=1. \end{align} \] The entry \(x_i\) represents the probability of occupying state \(i\).

NoteDefinition: Column-Stochastic Matrix

A matrix \(\bP \in \fR^{n \times n}\) is column-stochastic if:

  1. \(P_{ij} \geq 0\) for all \(i,j\).

  2. \(\sum_{i=1}^n P_{ij} = 1\) for each column \(j\).

TipRemark

(Column convention) Column \(j\) of \(\bP\) contains the transition probabilities from state \(j\) to all destination states \(i\). The update rule for a probability distribution is \(\bx^{(k+1)} = \bP \bx^{(k)}\).

NoteTheorem: Spectrum of a Stochastic Matrix

If \(\bP\) is column-stochastic, then \(\lambda=1\) is an eigenvalue, and every eigenvalue satisfies \(|\lambda|\leq 1\).

TipProof

The column sum condition implies \(\mathbf{1}^T\bP=\mathbf{1}^T\). Thus \(\lambda=1\) is a left eigenvalue with eigenvector \(\mathbf{1}^T\), which guarantees that \(1\) is an eigenvalue of \(\bP\).

To bound the spectral radius, let \(\bP^T\bv=\lambda\bv\) with \(\bv\neq \bzero\). Choose index \(j\) such that \(|v_j| = \|\bv\|_\infty = \max_i |v_i|\). Taking the \(j\)-th component of the eigenvalue equation yields \[ \begin{align} |\lambda|\,|v_j| = \left|\sum_{i=1}^n P_{ij}v_i\right| \leq \sum_{i=1}^n P_{ij}|v_i| \leq \left(\sum_{i=1}^n P_{ij}\right) |v_j| = |v_j|. \end{align} \] Dividing by \(|v_j|>0\) gives \(|\lambda|\leq 1\).

NoteDefinition: Stationary Distribution

A probability vector \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) is stationary if \(\bP \boldsymbol{\pi} = \boldsymbol{\pi}\). It is a right eigenvector of \(\bP\) associated with \(\lambda=1\), normalized so that \(\mathbf{1}^T\boldsymbol{\pi}=1\).

NoteTheorem: Perron–Frobenius for Markov Chains

If \(\bP\) is irreducible (every state can be reached from any other state in finitely many steps) and primitive (aperiodic, so \(\bP^k > 0\) elementwise for some \(k \geq 1\)), then:

  1. \(\lambda_1 = 1\) is an algebraically and geometrically simple eigenvalue.

  2. \(|\lambda_i| < 1\) for all other eigenvalues \(\lambda_i \neq 1\).

  3. The stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) is strictly positive in every entry.

  4. For any initial probability vector \(\bx^{(0)}\), \(\lim_{k\to\infty} \bP^k \bx^{(0)} = \boldsymbol{\pi}\).

NoteDefinition: Spectral Gap and Mixing Time

For a primitive chain with eigenvalues ordered as \(1 = \lambda_1 > |\lambda_2| \geq ... \geq |\lambda_n|\), the spectral gap is \[ \begin{align} \delta = 1 - |\lambda_2|. \end{align} \] For a diagonalizable matrix, the error \(\|\bx^{(k)} - \boldsymbol{\pi}\|_2\) decays asymptotically as \(\mathcal{O}(|\lambda_2|^k)\). The number of steps \(k_\varepsilon\) required to reach error tolerance \(\varepsilon\) satisfies \[ \begin{align} k_\varepsilon \approx \frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\delta}. \end{align} \]

NoteDefinition: Detailed Balance (Reversibility)

A Markov chain satisfies detailed balance with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) if \[ \begin{align} P_{ij} \pi_j = P_{ji} \pi_i \qquad \text{for all } i, j. \end{align} \] A chain satisfying detailed balance is reversible.

NoteTheorem: Real Spectrum of Reversible Chains

Let \(\bP\) satisfy detailed balance with stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol{\pi} > 0\). Define \(\bD_{\boldsymbol{\pi}} = \operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\pi})\). Then the matrix \[ \begin{align} \bS = \bD_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{-1/2} \bP \bD_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{1/2} \end{align} \] is symmetric. Consequently, all eigenvalues of \(\bP\) are real, and \(\bP\) has an orthogonal basis of eigenvectors in the inner product weighted by \(\bD_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{-1}\).

TipProof

The \((i,j)\) entry of \(\bS\) is \[ \begin{align} S_{ij} = \pi_i^{-1/2} P_{ij} \pi_j^{1/2} = \frac{P_{ij}\pi_j}{\sqrt{\pi_i\pi_j}}. \end{align} \] By detailed balance, \(P_{ij}\pi_j = P_{ji}\pi_i\). Substituting this equality gives \[ \begin{align} S_{ij} = \frac{P_{ji}\pi_i}{\sqrt{\pi_i\pi_j}} = \pi_j^{-1/2} P_{ji} \pi_i^{1/2} = S_{ji}. \end{align} \] Thus \(\bS = \bS^T\). Because \(\bP\) is similar to the real symmetric matrix \(\bS\), its eigenvalues are real.

34.2 Continuous-Time Markov Chains and the CME

NoteDefinition: Continuous-Time Infinitesimal Generator

A continuous-time Markov jump process on a discrete state space evolves according to \[ \begin{align} \frac{d}{dt}\bp(t) = \bA \bp(t), \end{align} \] where \(\bp(t)\) is the probability distribution vector and \(\bA\) is an infinitesimal generator matrix satisfying:

  1. \(A_{ij} \geq 0\) for all \(i \neq j\) (transition rates between distinct states are nonnegative).

  2. \(\sum_{i} A_{ij} = 0\) for every column \(j\) (column sums vanish).

  3. \(A_{jj} = -\sum_{i \neq j} A_{ij} \leq 0\) (diagonal entries equal the negative total exit rate from state \(j\)).

NoteDefinition: Chemical Master Equation (CME)

Consider a chemically reacting system with \(S\) molecular species and \(R\) reaction channels. The discrete state \(\bx \in \mathbb{N}_0^S\) records the copy number of each species. Each reaction channel \(k \in \{1,...,R\}\) is characterized by a stoichiometric change vector \(\bnu_k \in \mathbb{Z}^S\) and a propensity function \(\alpha_k(\bx; \bc) \geq 0\) parameterized by rate constants \(\bc\).

The Chemical Master Equation governs the probability \(p(\bx, t)\) of occupying state \(\bx\) at time \(t\): \[ \begin{align} \frac{\partial p(\bx, t)}{\partial t} = \sum_{k=1}^R \Big[ \alpha_k(\bx - \bnu_k; \bc)\, p(\bx - \bnu_k, t) - \alpha_k(\bx; \bc)\, p(\bx, t) \Big]. \end{align} \] Enumerating the reachable states yields the linear system of ordinary differential equations \[ \begin{align} \dot{\bp}(t) = \bA(\bc) \bp(t), \qquad \bp(0) = \bp_0, \end{align} \] whose exact formal solution is the matrix exponential action \(\bp(t) = \exp(t\bA(\bc)) \bp_0\).

34.3 Finite State Projection (FSP)

TipRemark

(Infinite state bottleneck) The CME generator \(\bA(\bc)\) is defined over an infinite or very large discrete state space \(\mathbb{N}_0^S\). A finite computation therefore requires truncation, aggregation, or another representation that avoids enumerating the full state space.

NoteDefinition: Finite State Projection (FSP)

Let the discrete state space be partitioned into a finite retained index set \(J \subset \mathbb{N}_0^S\) with \(|J| = K\), and an infinite or omitted complement set \(J^c\). Permuting states so that \(J\) appears first partitions the full generator: \[ \begin{align} \bA = \begin{pmatrix} \bA_J & \bA_{J, J^c} \\ \bA_{J^c, J} & \bA_{J^c} \end{pmatrix}. \end{align} \] The Finite State Projection approximates the true marginal probability on \(J\) by solving the isolated subgenerator system \[ \begin{align} \dot{\bp}_J(t) = \bA_J \bp_J(t), \qquad \bp_J(0) = \bp_0|_J. \end{align} \] Here \(\bA_J\) has negative diagonal entries and nonnegative off-diagonal entries, but its column sums are strictly nonpositive because transitions into \(J^c\) act as probability leaks.

NoteTheorem: FSP 1-Norm Leakage Bound

Let \(\bp(t)\) be the exact probability distribution solving \(\dot{\bp} = \bA\bp\) with initial condition supported on \(J\), so that \(\mathbf{1}^T\bp(t) = 1\). Let \(\bp_J(t) = \exp(t\bA_J)\bp_0|_J\) be the FSP solution. Then:

  1. Pointwise underestimation: \(\bzero \leq \bp_J(t) \leq \bp|_J(t)\) for all \(t \geq 0\).

  2. The full-space error of the zero-padded FSP approximation equals the leaked mass: \[ \begin{align} \|\bp(t) - \widetilde{\bp}_J(t)\|_1 = 1 - \mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(t), \end{align} \] where \(\widetilde{\bp}_J(t)\) is \(\bp_J(t)\) padded with zeros on \(J^c\). The retained-state error satisfies \[ \begin{align} \|\bp|_J(t)-\bp_J(t)\|_1 =\mathbf{1}^T\bp|_J(t)-\mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(t) \leq 1-\mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(t). \end{align} \]

TipProof

The exact retained dynamics satisfy the non-autonomous subgenerator ODE \[ \begin{align} \frac{d}{dt}\bp|_J(t) = \bA_J\bp|_J(t) + \bA_{J,J^c}\bp|_{J^c}(t), \qquad \bp|_J(0) = \bp_0|_J. \end{align} \] The FSP approximation satisfies \(\frac{d}{dt}\bp_J(t) = \bA_J\bp_J(t)\) with the same initial condition \(\bp_J(0) = \bp_0|_J\). Subtracting the two equations gives the defect ODE for the difference \(\boldsymbol{\delta}_J(t) = \bp|_J(t) - \bp_J(t)\): \[ \begin{align} \frac{d}{dt}\boldsymbol{\delta}_J(t) = \bA_J \boldsymbol{\delta}_J(t) + \bA_{J,J^c}\bp|_{J^c}(t), \qquad \boldsymbol{\delta}_J(0) = \bzero. \end{align} \] By Duhamel’s formula (variation of constants): \[ \begin{align} \boldsymbol{\delta}_J(t) = \bp|_J(t) - \bp_J(t) = \int_0^t e^{(t-s)\bA_J}\bA_{J,J^c}\bp|_{J^c}(s)\,ds. \end{align} \] Because \(\bA_J\) has non-negative off-diagonal entries, it is a Metzler matrix, and its matrix exponential \(e^{\tau\bA_J}\) is entrywise non-negative for all \(\tau \geq 0\). Furthermore, the coupling matrix \(\bA_{J, J^c} \geq \bzero\) and exact probabilities \(\bp|_{J^c}(s) \geq \bzero\) are non-negative. Consequently, the integrand is entrywise non-negative, proving that \[ \begin{align} \bp|_J(t) - \bp_J(t) \geq \bzero \implies \bzero \leq \bp_J(t) \leq \bp|_J(t) \quad \text{for all } t \geq 0. \end{align} \]

Because \(\bp_J(t) \leq \bp|_J(t)\), the marginal 1-norm difference on \(J\) simplifies without absolute value signs: \[ \begin{align} \|\bp|_J(t) - \bp_J(t)\|_1 = \sum_{i \in J} \big( p_i(t) - [\bp_J(t)]_i \big) = \mathbf{1}^T\bp|_J(t) - \mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(t). \end{align} \] The total probability across the full space satisfies \(\mathbf{1}^T\bp|_J(t) + \mathbf{1}^T\bp|_{J^c}(t) = 1\). The omitted probability mass on \(J^c\) is exactly \(1 - \mathbf{1}^T\bp|_J(t)\). Adding the unmodeled mass on \(J^c\) gives \[ \begin{align} \|\bp(t) - \widetilde{\bp}_J(t)\|_1 &= \|\bp|_J(t) - \bp_J(t)\|_1 + \|\bp|_{J^c}(t)\|_1 \\ &= \big(\mathbf{1}^T\bp|_J(t) - \mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(t)\big) + \big(1 - \mathbf{1}^T\bp|_J(t)\big) \\ &= 1 - \mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(t). \end{align} \] Since total variation distance is one half of the \(1\)-norm distance, the zero-padded approximation has total variation error \((1-\mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(t))/2\). A sink-state comparison uses a different state space and must be stated separately.

34.4 Truncation Strategy: Probability Flux versus Probability Mass

TipRemark

(Failure of instantaneous mass truncation) A naive heuristic for expanding or pruning states in the FSP retains states where the instantaneous probability \(p_i(t)\) exceeds a threshold \(\varepsilon\). In multiscale or stiff reaction networks, this heuristic can discard a low-mass intermediate that carries substantial probability flux and thereby produce an order-one error.

NoteDefinition: Probability Flux

For a transition from state \(j\) to state \(i\) with rate \(A_{ij} > 0\), the instantaneous probability flux at time \(t\) is \[ \begin{align} \Phi_{ij}(t) = A_{ij} p_j(t). \end{align} \] The cumulative probability flux entering state \(i\) over the time interval \([0, T]\) is \[ \begin{align} F_i(T) = \int_0^T \sum_{j \neq i} A_{ij} p_j(s)\, ds. \end{align} \]

TipRemark

(Transient intermediate states) Consider a reaction cascade \(S_1 \xrightarrow{k_1} S_2 \xrightarrow{k_2} S_3\) with \(k_2 \gg k_1\). State \(S_2\) has a rapid exit rate, so its instantaneous probability is tiny: \(p_2(t) \approx \frac{k_1}{k_2} p_1(t) \ll 1\). Pruning based on instantaneous mass \(p_2(t) < \varepsilon\) deletes \(S_2\) from the state space. However, every reaction producing \(S_3\) must pass through \(S_2\). Deleting \(S_2\) severs the probability flow entirely, causing an \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) error in \(p_3(T)\).

Robust adaptive FSP algorithms monitor cumulative probability flux rather than instantaneous probability mass. A state may have negligible instantaneous mass yet carry substantial probability flux across the network.

34.5 Exercises

WarningExercise

  1. Compute. (Discrete spectrum and mixing) Under the column-stochastic convention, let \(\bP=\begin{pmatrix}0.8&0.1\\0.2&0.9\end{pmatrix}\). Find its stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\), its second eigenvalue, and the spectral gap \(\delta\). Starting from \(\bx^{(0)}=\be_1\), derive the exact formula for \(\|\bP^k\bx^{(0)}-\boldsymbol{\pi}\|_2\). Compare the first \(k\) for which this error is at most \(10^{-3}\) with the estimate \(\log(10^3)/\delta\), and explain why the latter is only an asymptotic rule.

  2. Compute. (Detailed balance) Consider the column-stochastic matrix \[ \begin{align} \bP=\begin{pmatrix}0.6&0.2&0\\0.4&0.5&0.1\\0&0.3&0.9\end{pmatrix}. \end{align} \] Find its stationary distribution \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\), verify detailed balance on each edge, and compute \(\bS = \bD_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{-1/2}\bP\bD_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{1/2}\). Verify directly that \(\bS\) is symmetric and that the eigenvalues of \(\bP\) are real.

  3. Derive. (FSP 1-norm leakage bound derivation) Consider a CTMC with generator \(\bA\) partitioned into retained set \(J\) and complement \(J^c\).

    1. Prove that \(\mathbf{1}^T\bA_J \leq \bzero^T\) elementwise, with strict inequality for at least one entry if transitions from \(J\) to \(J^c\) exist.

    2. Show that \(\frac{d}{dt}\big(\mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(t)\big) \leq 0\), confirming that total modeled probability mass decreases monotonically over time.

    3. Let \(\varepsilon=1-\mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(T)\). Verify from the result above that the zero-padded FSP error is exactly \(\varepsilon\) in the \(1\)-norm. Explain what additional identification of omitted states would be needed before comparing an absorbing sink with the exact distribution.

  4. Explore. (Probability mass versus cumulative flux in stiff cascades) Consider the three-state continuous-time Markov chain \[ \begin{align} X_1 \xrightarrow{k_1} X_2 \xrightarrow{k_2} X_3 \end{align} \] with \(k_1 = 1\), \(k_2 = 10^4\), and initial condition \(\bp(0) = (1, 0, 0)^T\).

    1. Solve the system analytically for \(p_1(t), p_2(t), p_3(t)\).

    2. Show that \(\max_{t \geq 0} p_2(t) \approx 10^{-4}\). If a threshold \(\varepsilon = 10^{-3}\) is used to prune states by instantaneous mass, state \(X_2\) is discarded at all times.

    3. Compute the cumulative flux \(\int_0^T k_1 p_1(s)\, ds\) entering \(X_2\) for \(T = 3\). Show that over \(95\%\) of the total system probability passes through \(X_2\) despite its negligible instantaneous mass.

    4. Explain why adaptive truncation based on cumulative probability flux preserves state \(X_2\) while mass-based thresholding disconnects the state space.

  5. Derive. (Birth–death process and infinite generator truncation) For a simple birth–death process with birth rate \(\lambda\) and death rate \(\mu x\), write down the tridiagonal subgenerator \(\bA_J\) for copy numbers \(x \in \{0, 1, ..., N\}\). Formulate the exit rate from boundary state \(N\) and derive the leakage rate \(\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{1}^T\bp_J(t)\) as a function of \(p_N(t)\).

ImportantLiterature trail: The original finite state projection argument

Read Brian Munsky and Mustafa Khammash’s 2006 paper, The Finite State Projection Algorithm for the Solution of the Chemical Master Equation (Munsky and Khammash 2006).

Search hint. The exact title and authors lead directly to the Journal of Chemical Physics article.

Mathematical hint. Be careful about row-vector versus column-vector conventions and about whether the approximation is zero-padded or augmented by a sink. These choices change the form in which the error certificate is stated.

  1. Give a complete citation and locate the paper’s central FSP theorem.

  2. Translate its generator, probability vector, retained set, and error parameter into this chapter’s convention.

  3. State the positivity and generator assumptions that make the comparison argument work.

  4. Reconstruct the step that turns missing probability mass into an error certificate. Then compare the paper’s statement with the result above, identifying exactly which conclusions are identical and which depend on the chosen state-space representation.

NoteFurther reading

The finite-state projection method and its error certificate originate with Munsky and Khammash (Munsky and Khammash 2006). Higham’s treatment of matrix functions is useful background for the exponential calculations used here (Higham 2008).

Munsky, Brian, and Mustafa Khammash. 2006. “The Finite State Projection Algorithm for the Solution of the Chemical Master Equation.” The Journal of Chemical Physics 124 (4): 044104. https://doi.org/10.1063/1.2145882.
